{{short description|Phase transition in the two-dimensional (2-D) XY model}}
{{More footnotes|date=November 2019}}

The '''Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless''' ('''BKT''') '''transition''' is a [[phase transition]] of the two-dimensional (2-D) [[XY model]] in [[statistical physics]]. It is a transition from bound vortex-antivortex pairs at low temperatures to unpaired vortices and anti-vortices at some critical temperature. The transition is named for [[condensed matter physics|condensed matter]] physicists [[Vadim Berezinskii]], [[John M. Kosterlitz]] and [[David J. Thouless]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kosterlitz|first1=J. M.|last2=Thouless|first2=D. J.|date=November 1972|title=Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems|journal=Journal of Physics C: Solid State Physics|language=en|volume=6|issue=7|pages=1181–1203|doi=10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010|bibcode=1973JPhC....6.1181K |issn=0022-3719}}</ref>  BKT transitions can be found in several 2-D systems in condensed matter physics that are approximated by the XY model, including [[Josephson junction]] arrays and thin disordered [[superconducting]] granular films.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tinkham |first1=Michael |title=Introduction to Superconductivity |date=1906 |publisher=Dover Publications, INC. |location=Mineola, New York |isbn=0-486-43503-2 |pages=237–239 |edition=2.}}</ref> More recently, the term has been applied by the 2-D superconductor insulator transition community to the pinning of [[Cooper pair]]s in the insulating regime, due to similarities with the original vortex BKT transition.

The critical density of the BKT transition in the weakly interacting system reads<ref>{{cite book | url=https://link.springer.com/book/9789027714718 | title=Functional Integrals in Quantum Field Theory and Statistical Physics }}</ref>
: <math> n_\text{c} = \frac{mT}{2 \pi} \ln \frac{\xi}{mU}</math>
where the dimensionless constant was found to be <math> \xi = 380 \pm 3</math>.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.270402 | title=Critical Point of a Weakly Interacting Two-Dimensional Bose Gas | date=2001 | last1=Prokof'Ev | first1=Nikolay | last2=Ruebenacker | first2=Oliver | last3=Svistunov | first3=Boris | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=87 | issue=27 | article-number=270402 | pmid=11800861 | arxiv=cond-mat/0106075 | bibcode=2001PhRvL..87.0402P }}</ref>

Work on the transition led to the 2016 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] being awarded to Thouless and Kosterlitz; Berezinskii died in 1981.

== XY model ==
{{Main|Classical XY model}}
The [[XY model]] is a two-dimensional [[vector (geometric)|vector]] [[spin model]] that possesses [[U(1)]] or [[circular symmetry]]. This system is not expected to possess a normal [[phase transition|second-order phase transition]]. This is because the expected ordered phase of the system is destroyed by transverse fluctuations, i.e. the [[Goldstone boson|Nambu-Goldstone modes]] associated with this broken [[continuous symmetry]], which logarithmically diverge with system size.
This is a specific case of what is called the [[Mermin–Wagner theorem]] in spin systems.

Rigorously the transition is not completely understood, but the existence of two phases was proved by {{harvtxt|McBryan|Spencer|1977}} and {{harvtxt|Fröhlich|Spencer|1981}}.

=== Disordered phases with different correlations ===
In the XY model in two dimensions, a second-order phase transition is not seen. However, one finds a low-temperature quasi-ordered phase with a [[correlation function]] (see [[statistical mechanics]]) that decreases with the distance like a power, which depends on the temperature. The transition from the high-temperature disordered phase with the exponential correlation to this low-temperature quasi-ordered phase is a Kosterlitz–Thouless transition.
It is a [[phase transition]] of infinite order.

=== Role of vortices ===
In the 2-D XY model, [[quantum vortex|vortices]] are topologically stable configurations. It is found that the high-temperature disordered phase with exponential correlation decay is a result of the formation of vortices. Vortex generation becomes thermodynamically favorable at the critical temperature <math> T_\text{c}</math> of the Kosterlitz–Thouless transition. At temperatures below this, vortex generation has a power law correlation.

Kosterlitz–Thouless transitions is described as a dissociation of bound  vortex pairs with opposite circulations, called vortex–antivortex pairs, first described by [[Vadim Berezinskii]]. In these systems, thermal generation of vortices produces an even number of vortices of opposite sign. Bound vortex–antivortex pairs have lower energies than free vortices, but have lower entropy as well. In order to minimize free energy, <math>F=E-TS</math>, the system undergoes a transition at a critical temperature, <math> T_\text{c}</math>. Below <math> T_\text{c}</math>, there are only bound vortex–antivortex pairs. Above <math> T_\text{c}</math>, there are free vortices.

== Informal description ==
There is an elegant thermodynamic argument for the Kosterlitz–Thouless transition. The energy of a single vortex is <math>\kappa\ln(R/a)</math>, where <math>\kappa</math> is a parameter that depends upon the system in which the vortex is located, <math>R</math> is the system size, and <math>a</math> is the radius of the vortex core. One assumes <math>R\gg a</math>. In the 2D system, the number of possible positions of a vortex is approximately <math>(R/a)^2</math>. From [[Boltzmann's entropy formula]], <math> S= k_{\rm B} \ln W</math> (with W is the number of states), the [[entropy]] is <math>S=2k_{\rm B}\ln(R/a)</math>, where <math>k_{\rm B}</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]]. Thus, the [[Helmholtz free energy]] is
: <math>F = E - TS = (\kappa - 2k_{\rm B}T)\ln(R/a).</math>

When <math>F>0</math>, the system will not have a vortex. On the other hand, when <math>F<0</math>, entropic considerations favor the formation of a vortex. The critical temperature above which vortices may form can be found by setting <math> F=0 </math> and is given by
: <math>T_\text{c} = \frac{\kappa}{2k_{\rm B}}.</math>

The  Kosterlitz–Thouless transition can be observed experimentally in systems like 2D Josephson junction arrays by taking current and voltage (I-V) measurements. Above <math>T_\text{c}</math>, the relation will be linear <math>V \sim I</math>. Just below <math>T_c</math>, the relation will be <math>V \sim I^3</math>, as the number of free vortices will go as <math>I^2</math>. This jump from linear dependence is indicative of a  Kosterlitz–Thouless transition and may be used to determine <math>T_\text{c}</math>. This approach was used in Resnick et al.{{sfn|Resnick|Garland|Boyd|Shoemaker|1981}} to confirm the  Kosterlitz–Thouless transition in proximity-coupled [[Josephson junction]] arrays.

== Field theoretic analysis ==
The following discussion uses field theoretic methods. Assume a field φ(x) defined in the plane which takes on values in <math>S^1</math>, so that <math>\phi(x)</math> is identified with <math>\phi(x) + 2\pi</math>. That is, the circle is realized as <math>S^1 = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}</math>.

The energy is given by
: <math> E = \int \frac{1}{2} \nabla\phi\cdot\nabla\phi \, d^2 x</math>
and the [[Boltzmann factor]] is <math>\exp (-\beta E)</math>.

Taking a [[Methods of contour integration|contour integral]] <math>\textstyle \oint_\gamma d\phi = \oint_\gamma \frac{d\phi}{dx}dx</math> over any contractible closed path <math>\gamma</math>, we would expect it to be zero (for example, by the [[fundamental theorem of calculus]]). However, this is not the case due to the singular nature of vortices (which give singularities in <math>\phi</math>). 

To render the theory well-defined, it is only defined up to some energetic cut-off scale <math>\Lambda</math>, so that we can puncture the plane at the points where the vortices are located, by removing regions with size of order <math>1/\Lambda</math>. If <math>\gamma</math> winds counter-clockwise once around a puncture, the contour integral <math>\textstyle \oint_\gamma d\phi</math> is an integer multiple of <math>2\pi</math>. The value of this integer is the [[Vector_field#Index_of_a_vector_field|index]] of the vector field <math>\nabla \phi</math>.

Suppose that a given field configuration has <math>N</math> punctures located at <math>x_i, i=1,\dots,N</math> each with index <math>n_i=\pm 1</math>. Then, <math>\phi</math> decomposes into the sum of a field configuration with no punctures, <math>\phi_0</math> and <math>\textstyle \sum_{i=1}^N n_i\arg(z-z_i)</math>, where we have switched to the [[complex plane]] coordinates for convenience. The [[Argument (complex analysis)|complex argument]] function has a branch cut, but, because <math>\phi</math> is defined modulo <math>2\pi</math>, it has no physical consequences.

Now,
: <math>E = \int \frac{1}{2} \nabla\phi_0\cdot\nabla\phi_0 \, d^2 x + \sum_{1\leq i < j \leq N} n_i n_j \int \frac{1}{2} \nabla \ \arg(z-z_i)\cdot\nabla \arg(z-z_j) \, d^2 x</math>

If <math>\textstyle \sum_{i=1}^N n_i \neq 0</math>, the second term is positive and diverges in the limit <math>\Lambda \to \infty</math>: configurations with unbalanced numbers of vortices of each orientation are never energetically favoured.

However, if the ''neutral'' condition <math>\textstyle \sum_{i=1}^N n_i=0</math> holds, the second term is equal to <math>\textstyle -2\pi \sum_{1\leq i < j \leq N}  n_i n_j \ln(|x_j-x_i|/L)</math>, which is the total potential energy of a two-dimensional [[Coulomb gas]]. The scale ''L'' is an arbitrary scale that renders the argument of the logarithm dimensionless.

Assume the case with only vortices of multiplicity <math>\pm 1</math>. At low temperatures and large <math>\beta</math> the distance between a vortex and antivortex pair tends to be extremely small, essentially of the order <math>1/\Lambda</math>. At large temperatures and small <math>\beta</math> this distance increases, and the favoured configuration becomes effectively the one of a gas of free vortices and antivortices. The transition between the two different configurations is the Kosterlitz–Thouless phase transition, and the transition point is associated with an unbinding of vortex-antivortex pairs.
